---
title: "P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Water potential

### 1.1

Define *water potential* (Ψ), state its usual unit in plant physiology, and
give the water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Water potential is the chemical potential (free energy per unit volume) of
water relative to that of pure water at atmospheric pressure and the same
temperature. It is expressed in megapascals (MPa). Pure water at atmospheric
pressure has Ψ = 0 MPa.
:::

### 1.2

Arrange from the highest to the lowest water potential: −0.8 MPa, 0 MPa,
−1.5 MPa, −0.2 MPa. In which direction does water move passively?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

0 > −0.2 > −0.8 > −1.5 MPa. Water moves passively from higher (less negative)
to lower (more negative) water potential.
:::

### 1.3

Use Ψ = Ψs + Ψp (ignore gravity and matric potential). Both cells are placed in
the same external solution with Ψ = −0.4 MPa.

| Cell | Ψs (MPa) | Ψp (MPa) | Ψ (MPa) | Initial net water movement |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| A | −0.8 | +0.2 | | |
| B | −0.7 | +0.5 | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Cell | Ψs (MPa) | Ψp (MPa) | Ψ (MPa) | Initial net water movement |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| A | −0.8 | +0.2 | −0.6 | Into the cell (−0.4 > −0.6) |
| B | −0.7 | +0.5 | −0.2 | Out of the cell (−0.2 > −0.4) |

Cell B loses water even though its solute potential is more negative than the
external solution, because total Ψ determines direction.
:::

### 1.4

Calculate the solute potential at 25 °C (298 K) of

a. 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sucrose
b. 0.1 mol L⁻¹ NaCl (assume complete dissociation)

Use Ψs = −*cRT*, where *c* is the osmolar concentration and
*R* = 0.008314 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Ψs = −(0.1 mol L⁻¹)(0.008314 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)(298 K) = −0.25 MPa.
b. NaCl gives two particles, so *c* = 0.2 osmol L⁻¹ and Ψs = −0.50 MPa.
:::

### 1.5

A flaccid cell (Ψp = 0) has Ψs = −0.6 MPa. Assume the cell volume, and hence
Ψs, does not change.

a. What is its Ψ?
b. It is placed in pure water. What are Ψ and Ψp at equilibrium?
c. It is instead placed in a solution with Ψ = −0.8 MPa. In which direction does
   water move, and what is Ψp at the end?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Ψ = −0.6 + 0 = −0.6 MPa.
b. Water enters until Ψ = 0 MPa; then Ψp = 0 − (−0.6) = +0.6 MPa.
c. Water leaves the cell (−0.6 > −0.8). Ψp stays at 0 (it cannot become
   strongly negative in a living cell); the protoplast shrinks away from the
   wall (plasmolysis).
:::

### 1.6

A root cell has Ψ = −0.4 MPa. Give the initial direction of net water movement
between the cell and the soil solution when the soil solution has

a. Ψ = −0.1 MPa
b. Ψ = −0.6 MPa (saline soil)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. From soil into the root cell.
b. From the root cell into the soil. Saline soil can therefore cause water
   stress although it is wet.
:::

## Uptake by roots

### 2.1

Name the three routes by which water crosses the root cortex and state which
structure each route passes through.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Apoplastic:** through cell walls and intercellular spaces, without
  crossing membranes.
- **Symplastic:** from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata.
- **Transmembrane (transcellular):** across the plasma membrane (and tonoplast)
  of each successive cell.
:::

### 2.2

a. In which cell layer is the Casparian strip found?
b. Which compounds make it?
c. What is its function?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The endodermis, in the radial and transverse walls.
b. Suberin (with lignin).
c. It blocks the apoplastic route into the stele, so water and solutes must
   cross a plasma membrane, which allows selective uptake.
:::

### 2.3

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Aquaporins pump water into root cells using ATP.
b. The plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase uses ATP to build an electrochemical proton gradient.
c. A proton-coupled carrier can move a nutrient ion against its own concentration gradient.
d. Inhibiting the H⁺-ATPase directly stops passive water flow through aquaporins.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Aquaporins are channels that increase membrane permeability to water;
   water moves passively down its potential gradient.
b. True.
c. True. Energy comes from protons moving down their electrochemical gradient
   (secondary active transport).
d. False. It reduces proton-coupled solute uptake; water flow through
   aquaporins is passive and not directly driven by ATP.
:::

### 2.4

Waterlogged soil contains plenty of water, yet mineral uptake by roots falls.
Give the chain of causes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Water fills the soil pores → little O₂ reaches the roots → aerobic respiration
falls → less ATP → H⁺-ATPase activity and the proton gradient decline →
less active (proton-coupled) uptake of mineral ions.
:::

## Xylem transport and transpiration

### 3.1

Arrange the steps of water movement in a transpiring plant in order:

a. water vapour diffuses out through the stomatal pore
b. water crosses the root endodermis
c. water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces
d. water enters the root from the soil
e. water moves up the xylem under tension

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

d → b → e → c → a.
:::

### 3.2

Match each term to its definition: cohesion, adhesion, tension, cavitation.

1. Negative hydrostatic pressure in the xylem water
2. Attraction between water molecules through hydrogen bonding
3. Breakage of the water column and formation of a gas bubble in a conduit
4. Attraction between water molecules and the conduit walls

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Cohesion–2, adhesion–4, tension–1, cavitation–3. A gas-filled conduit after
cavitation is said to be embolised.
:::

### 3.3

Typical water potentials in a transpiring plant are listed. Arrange them in the
order water passes and state what drives the flow.

Leaf cells: −0.8 MPa. Soil: −0.1 MPa. Atmosphere (50 % relative humidity):
−95 MPa. Root xylem: −0.4 MPa.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Soil (−0.1) → root xylem (−0.4) → leaf cells (−0.8) → atmosphere (−95 MPa).
Water moves passively down this gradient of decreasing water potential. The
energy comes from evaporation at the leaf (ultimately solar energy); the plant
does not pump water.
:::

### 3.4

Four pots are weighed over 4 h. Unplanted soil controls lose 4 g per pot over
the same time.

| Pot | Mass loss (g) | Leaf area (m²) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 24 | 0.10 |
| 2 | 27 | 0.12 |
| 3 | 22 | 0.10 |
| 4 | 25 | 0.11 |

a. Calculate the transpiration rate of each pot in g m⁻² h⁻¹ after subtracting
   soil evaporation.
b. Calculate the mean rate.
c. Convert the rate of pot 1 to mmol H₂O m⁻² s⁻¹ (M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Rate = (loss − 4 g) / (4 h × leaf area).

| Pot | Corrected loss (g) | Rate (g m⁻² h⁻¹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 20 | 50.0 |
| 2 | 23 | 47.9 |
| 3 | 18 | 45.0 |
| 4 | 21 | 47.7 |

b. (50.0 + 47.9 + 45.0 + 47.7) / 4 = 47.7 g m⁻² h⁻¹.
c. 50 g m⁻² h⁻¹ ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 2.78 mol m⁻² h⁻¹; ÷ 3600 s h⁻¹ =
   7.7 × 10⁻⁴ mol m⁻² s⁻¹ = 0.77 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹.
:::

### 3.5

State whether each change increases or decreases the transpiration rate when
stomatal conductance stays the same.

a. Lower air humidity
b. Higher leaf temperature
c. Stronger wind removing the boundary layer
d. Smaller total leaf area

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Increases (larger vapour pressure difference between leaf and air).
b. Increases (higher vapour pressure inside the leaf).
c. Increases (thinner boundary layer, lower resistance).
d. Decreases (less evaporating surface per plant).
:::

## Stomata

### 4.1

Put the steps of light-induced stomatal opening in order:

a. guard-cell water potential falls
b. blue light activates the guard-cell plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase
c. turgor rises and the guard cells bow apart, opening the pore
d. K⁺ enters through inward-rectifying channels, with Cl⁻ uptake and malate synthesis
e. the membrane hyperpolarises
f. water enters the guard cells

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → e → d → a → f → c.
:::

### 4.2

State whether each condition causes stomata to open or close.

a. Blue light at dawn
b. High intercellular CO₂ concentration
c. Increased ABA in the leaf
d. Low intercellular CO₂ concentration
e. Low leaf water potential (drought)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Open. b. Close. c. Close. d. Open. e. Close.
:::

### 4.3

How does abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata? Give the sequence from ABA
perception to pore closure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

ABA binds receptors in the guard cells → anion channels open and anions leave →
the membrane depolarises → K⁺ leaves through outward-rectifying channels →
guard-cell Ψs and Ψ rise → water leaves → turgor falls → the pore closes.
ABA acts as a signal; it does not plug the pore.
:::

## Mineral nutrition

### 5.1

Define an *essential element*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

An element without which the plant cannot complete its life cycle, or which is
part of an essential molecule or structure of the plant; its function cannot be
replaced by another element.
:::

### 5.2

Classify each element as a macronutrient or a micronutrient: N, Fe, K, Zn, Mg,
Mo, P, Mn, S, Cu, Ca, B.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Macronutrients: N, K, Mg, P, S, Ca. Micronutrients: Fe, Zn, Mo, Mn, Cu, B.
The classification refers to the amount required, not to importance.
:::

### 5.3

Match each element to one role.

| | Element |
| --- | --- |
| A | Nitrogen |
| B | Phosphorus |
| C | Potassium |
| D | Magnesium |
| E | Iron |

Roles: (1) central atom of chlorophyll; (2) main cation for osmotic regulation,
e.g. in guard cells; (3) component of amino acids, proteins and nucleotides;
(4) component of cytochromes and Fe–S proteins in electron transport;
(5) component of ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A–3, B–5, C–2, D–1, E–4.
:::

### 5.4

Deficiency of nitrogen first causes yellowing of the older leaves, whereas iron
deficiency first causes yellowing of the young leaves. Explain the difference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Nitrogen is mobile in the phloem: it is remobilised from old leaves to new
growth, so old leaves show symptoms first. Iron is relatively immobile and
cannot be withdrawn from old leaves, so new leaves, which depend on current
uptake, show symptoms first.
:::

### 5.5

What does each partner gain in an arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The plant gains mineral nutrients, especially phosphate, and water taken up by
the fungal hyphae from a larger soil volume. The fungus gains carbon
(sugars and lipids) from the plant.
:::

## Explore: A plant cell in a solution {#explore-p2-waterpotential}

A flaccid plant cell is placed in a solution and exchanges water until its
water potential Ψ = Ψs + Ψp equals that of the solution. Choose a preset or
set the cell sap Ψs (at the flaccid volume), the solution Ψ and the wall
stiffness; the bars and the readout give Ψs, Ψp and Ψ at equilibrium, and the
label under the cell gives its state and protoplast volume.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p2-waterpotential"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p2-waterpotential.js"></script>
```

### E1.1

Click "Pure water" (cell sap Ψs −0.60 MPa, solution 0 MPa, wall stiffness
10 MPa). In which direction does water move, and what are Ψs, Ψp and Ψ of the
cell at equilibrium?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Water moves into the cell. At equilibrium Ψ = 0 MPa, with Ψp = +0.57 MPa and
Ψs = −0.57 MPa (the sap is slightly diluted as the protoplast swells to
1.06 × V₀). The cell is turgid.
:::

### E1.2

Click "−0.6 MPa" and then "−0.8 MPa". Give the state of the cell (turgid,
flaccid or plasmolysed) and its Ψp in each case.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

−0.6 MPa: flaccid, Ψp = 0, no net water flow (the solution equals the cell
sap). −0.8 MPa: plasmolysed, Ψp = 0; water leaves until Ψs has fallen to
−0.80 MPa, at a protoplast volume of 0.75 × V₀.
:::

### E1.3

Click "Saline soil": a root cell with Ψs = −0.40 MPa in a soil solution of
−0.60 MPa. Does the cell gain or lose water, and what is its protoplast volume
at equilibrium?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

It loses water (−0.40 > −0.60) and plasmolyses; the protoplast shrinks to
0.67 × V₀ so that Ψs reaches −0.60 MPa. Even in wet soil, salt can lower the
soil Ψ enough to draw water out of the root.
:::

### E1.4

Return to pure water (Ψs −0.60, solution 0) and compare wall stiffness 40 MPa
with 2 MPa. Which wall gives the higher Ψp at equilibrium, and which cell
swells more?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The stiff wall (40 MPa) gives the higher Ψp, +0.59 MPa, with almost no swelling
(1.01 × V₀). The soft wall (2 MPa) swells to 1.24 × V₀, which dilutes the sap
to −0.48 MPa, so Ψp is only +0.48 MPa.
:::

### E1.5

Keep the cell sap at −0.60 MPa and the wall at 10 MPa, and lower the solution
Ψ slowly from 0. Below which solution Ψ does plasmolysis begin?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Below −0.60 MPa, i.e. when the solution Ψ is lower than the Ψs of the cell sap
at the flaccid volume (incipient plasmolysis).
:::

## Explore: The soil–plant–air continuum {#explore-p2-soilplantair}

Steady-state transpiration through the chain soil → root → stem → leaf → air.
The vapour pressure deficit and stomatal opening set the flux; each
resistance along the path then lowers Ψ in proportion to it. Set humidity,
soil Ψ, plant height and stomatal opening, or click a preset; the plot shows
Ψ at each point, and the panel gives the transpiration rate.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p2-soilplantair"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p2-soilplantair.js"></script>
```

### E2.1

Click "Lecture" (50 % humidity, soil −0.10 MPa, 1 m, stomata fully open). Give
the transpiration rate, Ψ of the leaf cells and Ψ of the air. Where along the
path is the largest drop in water potential?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Transpiration 6.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹, leaf cells −0.83 MPa, air −95 MPa. The largest
drop is between the leaf and the air (about 94 MPa), in the vapour phase, far
larger than any drop in the liquid path.
:::

### E2.2

Click "Humid" (90 % humidity). Does transpiration increase or decrease, and is
the leaf Ψ higher or lower than at 50 %? What happens at 100 % humidity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Transpiration decreases to 1.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (the vapour pressure deficit falls
from 1.58 to 0.32 kPa), and the leaf Ψ is higher, −0.25 MPa. At 100 %
humidity the deficit is zero, transpiration stops and the profile is flat at
the soil value.
:::

### E2.3

Click "Dry soil" (soil −0.80 MPa, stomata do not respond), then "Dry soil +
ABA". Give the transpiration rate and the leaf Ψ in each case.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Dry soil: 6.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and leaf Ψ −5.47 MPa, far below the wilting line;
the xylem would cavitate. Dry soil + ABA: stomata partly close (conductance
89 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹), transpiration falls to 1.4 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and the leaf stays
at −1.85 MPa. The plant saves water at the cost of CO₂ uptake.
:::

### E2.4

Use the "Lecture" settings and halve stomatal opening to 50 %. By what factor
does transpiration change, and does the leaf Ψ rise or fall?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Transpiration halves, from 6.3 to 3.1 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹; the leaf Ψ rises from
−0.83 to −0.47 MPa because less water flows through the resistances.
:::

### E2.5

Click "Redwood" (100 m tall). How much water potential does gravity alone
cost over that height, according to the panel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

0.98 MPa (0.0098 MPa per metre × 100 m), before any loss due to flow.
:::

## Bioinformatics and R {#bioinformatics}

A plant has not one aquaporin or one nitrate transporter but whole **gene
families** of them, and the members are switched on in different organs. In
these exercises you find the members of a family in UniProt, look up where each
one is expressed in an **expression atlas**, and use R to read the real
expression table, rank the genes and model transport. The R code uses base R
only and reads the data straight from the databases, so you need an internet
connection. Run each block in R or RStudio and read the answer off the output.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to search a gene family and an expression atlas

**Gene family in UniProt** (recap of A1). At
[uniprot.org](https://www.uniprot.org) a family can be searched with the
`family:` field, combined with an organism and the Reviewed filter, e.g.
`family:aquaporin AND organism_id:3702 AND reviewed:true` (3702 is the NCBI
taxonomy ID of *Arabidopsis thaliana*). The entry's **Family & Domains** section
names the family and subfamily, and its **Expression** section gives the
annotated *Tissue specificity*. Arabidopsis genes are also named by their AGI
code (AT + chromosome + G + number, e.g. AT2G37170 = chromosome 2), shown under
*Names & Taxonomy* and in the TAIR cross-reference.

**Expression Atlas** ([www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa)) collects
RNA-seq experiments that were reanalysed in one pipeline. Type a gene name or
AGI code (e.g. `AT5G60660`) with species *Arabidopsis thaliana*; the
**Baseline expression** tab shows one row per experiment and one coloured cell
per tissue, with the value in **TPM** (transcripts per million: the share of
all mRNA molecules, so values can be compared between genes in the same
sample). A blank cell means expression below the detection cut-off. Clicking an
experiment opens its full table; the **Downloads** button gives the whole table
as a tab-separated file, which R can read directly. Here we use experiment
[E-GEOD-38612](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa/experiments/E-GEOD-38612/Results)
(leaf, flower, fruit and root of Col-0 Arabidopsis).

**eFP browser / ePlant** ([bar.utoronto.ca/efp](https://bar.utoronto.ca/efp/cgi-bin/efpWeb.cgi),
[ePlant](https://bar.utoronto.ca/eplant/)) shows the same kind of data as a
picture of the plant coloured by expression; enter an AGI code and choose a
data source such as "Developmental Map". Use it to check your R results by eye.

To compare two organs use the ratio on a log₂ scale:
log₂(root/leaf) = +3 means 8 times higher in root, −3 means 8 times higher in
leaf. Adding 1 TPM to both before dividing avoids dividing by zero.
:::

### B1. How many water channels does a plant need?

The water channels of plants belong to the MIP/aquaporin family. Run the code,
which downloads all reviewed Arabidopsis members from UniProt and counts them
per subfamily.

```r
url <- paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?",
  "query=organism_id:3702+AND+reviewed:true+AND+family:aquaporin",
  "&fields=accession,gene_primary,protein_families,xref_tair&format=tsv")
mip <- read.delim(url)
nrow(mip)
mip$subfamily <- sub(".*family, ([A-Z]+) .*", "\\1", mip$Protein.families)
table(mip$subfamily)
```

a. How many reviewed MIP/aquaporin proteins does Arabidopsis have?
b. Which subfamily is the largest, and how many members does it have?
c. PIP stands for *plasma membrane intrinsic protein* and TIP for *tonoplast
   intrinsic protein*. Which subfamily would you expect in the membrane of the
   central vacuole?
d. Open the UniProt entry of NIP5-1 (Q9SV84) and read its Function. Which
   substance does it mainly transport?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
nrow(mip)
## [1] 35
table(mip$subfamily)
## NIP PIP SIP TIP
##   9  13   3  10
```

a. 35.
b. PIP, with 13 members.
c. TIP (the tonoplast is the vacuolar membrane). The large vacuole fills most of
   a plant cell, so water must cross both membranes: PIPs at the plasma
   membrane and TIPs at the tonoplast.
d. Boric acid ("boric acid channel for the boron uptake required for plant
   growth and development under boron limitation"). Members of the aquaporin
   family are not all water channels: some take up the micronutrient boron.
:::

### B2. Which aquaporin serves the root and which the leaf?

Water enters the plant across root cell membranes and leaves it from the
mesophyll, so you might expect different PIPs in the two organs. Run the code.
It repeats the UniProt download, keeps the 13 PIPs, reads the Expression Atlas
table for E-GEOD-38612 (about 28 000 genes) and sorts the PIPs by
log₂(root/leaf).

```r
url <- paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?",
  "query=organism_id:3702+AND+reviewed:true+AND+family:aquaporin",
  "&fields=accession,gene_primary,protein_families,xref_tair&format=tsv")
mip <- read.delim(url)
mip$subfamily <- sub(".*family, ([A-Z]+) .*", "\\1", mip$Protein.families)
mip$agi <- sub(";", "", mip$TAIR)
atlas <- read.delim(paste0("https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa/experiments-content/",
  "E-GEOD-38612/resources/ExperimentDownloadSupplier.RnaSeqBaseline/tpmss.tsv"),
  comment.char = "#")
pip <- mip[mip$subfamily == "PIP", c("Gene.Names..primary.", "agi")]
pip <- cbind(pip, atlas[match(pip$agi, atlas$Gene.ID), c("leaf", "root")])
pip$log2_root_leaf <- round(log2((pip$root + 1) / (pip$leaf + 1)), 1)
pip <- pip[order(pip$log2_root_leaf), ]
pip
barplot(pip$log2_root_leaf, names.arg = pip$Gene.Names..primary., las = 2,
        ylab = "log2(root / leaf)")
```

a. Which PIP is the most root-biased?
b. Which PIP is the most leaf-biased?
c. Which PIP has the second-highest root bias? Open its UniProt entry
   (P43287) and read *Tissue specificity*: in which three root tissues is it
   strongly expressed?
d. Search Expression Atlas or the eFP browser for the most leaf-biased PIP
   from (b). Is it also low in roots in the other experiments shown (yes/no)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
pip
##    Gene.Names..primary.       agi leaf root log2_root_leaf
## 32               PIP2-6 AT2G39010  283    5           -5.6
## 16               PIP1.4 AT4G00430  186   37           -2.3
## 31               PIP2-5 AT3G54820   11    7           -0.6
## 33               PIP2-8 AT2G16850   21   15           -0.5
## 6                PIP2-7 AT4G35100  600  495           -0.3
## 8                PIP1-3 AT1G01620  509  475           -0.1
## 24               PIP1-5 AT4G23400  292  350            0.3
## 7                PIP1-2 AT2G45960 1229 1700            0.5
## 3                PIP2-1 AT3G53420  642 1132            0.8
## 2                PIP2-3 AT2G37180   26   96            1.8
## 5                PIP1-1 AT3G61430 1269  299            2.1
## 4                PIP2-2 AT2G37170  118  925            3.0
## 27               PIP2-4 AT5G60660    2  102            5.1
```

(Row numbers and the exact TPM values may differ slightly if the atlas is
reanalysed; the ranking at the two ends is the same in other Arabidopsis
tissue atlases.)

a. PIP2;4 (AT5G60660), about 35 times higher in root than in leaf.
b. PIP2;6 (AT2G39010), about 50 times higher in leaf than in root.
c. PIP2;2 (AT2G37170); UniProt: "predominantly expressed in the root, with a
   strong expression in the cortex, endodermis, and stele", i.e. along the
   radial path water takes to the xylem. Its Function adds that it has a
   predominant role in root water uptake.
d. Yes. Several PIPs (PIP1;2, PIP2;1, PIP2;7) are high everywhere and act as
   general water channels, while a few paralogues specialise in one organ.
:::

### B3. Same channel, different address

Paralogues are copies of a gene within one genome, formed by duplication.
Compare two pairs of PIP paralogues: PIP2;2 (P43287, AT2G37170) with PIP2;3
(P30302, AT2G37180), and the root-type PIP2;4 (Q9FF53) with the leaf-type
PIP2;6 (Q9ZV07).

a. Look at the AGI codes of PIP2;2 and PIP2;3. What do they tell you about
   where the two genes lie in the genome, and what kind of duplication does
   this suggest?
b. Align each pair with
   [EMBOSS Needle](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/psa/emboss_needle)
   (choose Protein and paste the two FASTA sequences, which you get from
   `https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/<accession>.fasta`; the output gives
   *Identity* in %). Which pair has the higher percent identity?
c. Run the code. Do PIP2;4 and PIP2;6 both keep the two NPA motifs that form
   the water pore (yes/no), and do the positions agree with the *Motif*
   features in UniProt (Family & Domains)?

```r
get_seq <- function(acc) {
  fa <- readLines(paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/", acc, ".fasta"))
  paste(fa[-1], collapse = "")
}
pip24 <- get_seq("Q9FF53")   # PIP2;4, root
pip26 <- get_seq("Q9ZV07")   # PIP2;6, leaf
nchar(c(PIP2.4 = pip24, PIP2.6 = pip26))
gregexpr("NPA", pip24)[[1]][1:2]
gregexpr("NPA", pip26)[[1]][1:2]
```

d. Which statement best explains why PIP2;4 works in roots and PIP2;6 in
   leaves?
   A. PIP2;6 has lost its water pore.
   B. The two proteins are similar channels; their genes differ in the
      regulatory sequences that decide in which organ they are transcribed.
   C. Leaves do not need water channels.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. They have neighbouring AGI numbers on chromosome 2 (…37170 and …37180), so
   the genes lie next to each other: a tandem duplication.
b. PIP2;2 and PIP2;3 (about 97 % identity) are far more similar than PIP2;4
   and PIP2;6 (about 75 %). The tandem pair arose recently; both copies are
   still root-biased (B2).
c. Yes.

   ```r
   nchar(c(PIP2.4 = pip24, PIP2.6 = pip26))
   ## PIP2.4 PIP2.6
   ##    291    289
   gregexpr("NPA", pip24)[[1]][1:2]
   ## [1] 107 228
   gregexpr("NPA", pip26)[[1]][1:2]
   ## [1] 106 227
   ```

   The positions match UniProt (NPA 1 at 107–109 and NPA 2 at 228–230 in
   PIP2;4; 106–108 and 227–229 in PIP2;6).
d. B. After duplication the copies kept the channel but diverged in where
   they are expressed, so the plant can tune water permeability organ by organ.
:::

### B4. Genes the root needs and the leaf does not

Roots take up mineral nutrients and build the Casparian strip; leaves fix CO₂.
Run the code, which ranks six genes by root bias in the same atlas.

```r
atlas <- read.delim(paste0("https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa/experiments-content/",
  "E-GEOD-38612/resources/ExperimentDownloadSupplier.RnaSeqBaseline/tpmss.tsv"),
  comment.char = "#")
genes <- c(CASP1 = "AT2G36100", IRT1 = "AT4G19690", FRO2 = "AT1G01580",
           PHT1.1 = "AT5G43350", NPF6.3 = "AT1G12110", RBCS1A = "AT1G67090")
x <- atlas[match(genes, atlas$Gene.ID), c("leaf", "root")]
x[is.na(x)] <- 0          # blank in the atlas = below detection
rownames(x) <- names(genes)
x$log2_root_leaf <- round(log2((x$root + 1) / (x$leaf + 1)), 1)
x[order(-x$log2_root_leaf), ]
```

a. Which gene is strongly leaf-biased, and what does it encode (search it in
   UniProt or Expression Atlas)?
b. Which root-biased gene is still expressed above 10 TPM in leaves?
c. Use the *Function* and *Tissue specificity* in UniProt. In which root cell
   layer does CASP1 act, and in which does IRT1 take up iron?
d. FRO2 works just before IRT1. What does FRO2 do to iron in the soil?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
x[order(-x$log2_root_leaf), ]
##           leaf root log2_root_leaf
## IRT1       0.5  500            8.4
## CASP1      0.6  212            7.1
## FRO2       0.8  209            6.9
## PHT1.1     3.0  133            5.1
## NPF6.3    29.0  204            2.8
## RBCS1A 16803.0  107           -7.3
```

a. RBCS1A, a Rubisco small subunit: one of the most abundant leaf mRNAs
   (about 17 000 TPM), almost absent from roots.
b. NPF6.3 (NRT1.1, the nitrate transporter), 29 TPM in leaves. UniProt notes
   it also in young leaves and guard cells.
c. CASP1: the endodermis (it positions the Casparian strip). IRT1: the root
   epidermis (outer cell layers).
d. It reduces ferric iron (Fe³⁺) chelates to soluble ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), the
   form IRT1 transports. The nutrient genes and CASP1 are almost root-only
   because only the root faces the soil.
:::

### B5. A nitrate transporter with two gears

NPF6.3 (NRT1.1, UniProt Q05085) can work in a high-affinity or a
low-affinity mode. Open the UniProt entry and read *Function*, *PTM /
Processing* (Modified residue and PTM comment, plus Mutagenesis) and
*Biophysicochemical properties*.

a. Which residue is phosphorylated, and by which kinase? Run the first part
   of the code to confirm that this residue is in the sequence.
b. What are the Km values for nitrate of the high-affinity and the
   low-affinity phase?
c. Run the second part, which uses the Michaelis–Menten equation
   v/Vmax = S/(Km + S) with these Km values (assume the same Vmax in both
   modes). At 0.1 mM nitrate, a typical value in poor soil, what fraction of
   Vmax does each mode reach?
d. In the mutant T101A the residue cannot be phosphorylated. Which mode is lost?
e. True or false: low nitrogen in the medium stimulates phosphorylation, which
   switches the transporter into the mode that suits a poor soil.

```r
# part 1: the sequence
fa <- readLines("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q05085.fasta")
nrt11 <- paste(fa[-1], collapse = "")
nchar(nrt11)
substr(nrt11, 101, 101)
substr(nrt11, 96, 106)

# part 2: uptake in the two modes
Km_high <- 0.049   # mM
Km_low  <- 4       # mM
nitrate <- c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)   # mM in the soil solution
data.frame(nitrate,
           high = round(nitrate / (Km_high + nitrate), 2),
           low  = round(nitrate / (Km_low  + nitrate), 2))
s <- 10^seq(-2, 1, length.out = 200)
plot(s, s / (Km_high + s), type = "l", log = "x",
     xlab = "Nitrate (mM)", ylab = "Uptake (fraction of Vmax)")
lines(s, s / (Km_low + s), lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("phosphorylated (high affinity)",
                    "dephosphorylated (low affinity)"), lty = 1:2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
nchar(nrt11)
## [1] 590
substr(nrt11, 101, 101)
## [1] "T"
substr(nrt11, 96, 106)
## [1] "LGRYLTIAIFA"
data.frame(nitrate, high = ..., low = ...)
##   nitrate high  low
## 1    0.01 0.17 0.00
## 2    0.10 0.67 0.02
## 3    1.00 0.95 0.20
## 4   10.00 1.00 0.71
```

a. Threonine 101 (phosphothreonine), by the kinase CIPK23.
b. 49 µM (0.049 mM) for the high-affinity phase and 4 mM for the low-affinity
   phase.
c. High-affinity mode 0.67 of Vmax; low-affinity mode 0.02. At poor-soil
   concentrations only the high-affinity mode takes up nitrate at a useful
   rate; at 10 mM both modes approach Vmax.
d. The high-affinity mode (91 % reduction of high-affinity transport). The
   phospho-mimic T101D instead loses low-affinity transport.
e. True (UniProt PTM comment). One protein covers a 100-fold range of soil
   nitrate by a phosphorylation switch rather than by changing the gene.
:::
